prompt:
I need the front end for Releasewell. The in-house chart production workspace of a state labor department's labor market information office, where analysts, an editor and a disclosure reviewer prepare the charts for each monthly jobs report together.

Who's using it: Ana Delacroix, the senior economist who leads the monthly employment release. She drafts some charts herself and signs off on all of them before they go to the communications office.

What they're doing right now: It is Tuesday, two days before the October jobs report goes public Thursday at 8:30 a.m. under embargo. Four people are working on its 22 charts this afternoon. A revised set of September numbers came in this morning, so three analysts are updating their charts, and the disclosure reviewer has blocked two county-level charts because some industry cells in small counties fall below the confidentiality threshold. Ana needs to see who is editing what right now, what changed since she last looked, which charts still need her approval, respond to the editor's note about wording in a headline, and make sure no one other than her can mark a chart final or release it to communications.

What's in the system at this point: October 2026 release with 22 charts, each with a title, owner, data source (CES payroll survey, LAUS unemployment, QCEW), geography (statewide, 7 metro areas, 64 counties), status (drafting, in review, disclosure hold, approved, final), version number, last editor and time. 14 approved, 4 in review, 2 on disclosure hold, 2 drafting. Team of 6: Ana (lead, can finalize), 3 analysts (edit their own charts, comment on others), 1 editor (edits titles, notes and captions only), 1 disclosure reviewer (can place and lift holds). Currently active: 4 people, with who is on which chart. Change history per chart, e.g. statewide unemployment rate revised from 4.1% to 4.2% for September; nonfarm payroll change +6,300 jobs month-over-month. 17 open comments, 5 addressed to Ana. Embargo: Thursday Nov 19, 8:30 a.m.; handoff to communications Wednesday 5 p.m.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
